newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Taxes seen best way to cool HK housing market.
newsitem.headline: Taxes seen best way to cool HK housing market.

text.p: Taxes on short-term property trading would be the most effective way to curb rampant speculation in Hong Kong's housing sector, property analysts said on Tuesday.
"If you're wanting effectiveness (to control speculation), it has to be done through the taxation regime," Serena Lau, managing director at Francis Lau & Co (Surveyors), told Reuters.

Analysts said the introduction of capital gains tax or extra stamp duty on a property sale made within months of its purchase would the most effective way of taming speculation, often blamed as the key factor behind hefty prices.

On Saturday, C.Y. Leung, a property surveyor named by future leader Tung Chee-hwa as head of a post-colonial committee to map out long-term housing strategy, said he had completed a report outlining ideas to curb speculation.
He gave no details on his proposals but said they would not impact long-term investors or genuine home buyers.
The British colony of 6.4 million people returns to China at midnight on June 30.

Property prices have been soaring in the territory in past months, rebounding more than 10 percent since March when the government announced measures to curb prices that led to fall of about five to 12 percent, analysts said.
Property agents say most property prices rose by 20 to 30 percent last year.

Lau said the imposition of capital gains tax would be the quickest way to dampen the market. A tax of 10 percent of the profit from a sale made within two to three months of the property's purchase would be enough to discourage speculators.
Desmond Cheung, an analyst at Vickers Ballas, said capital gains tax was certain to hit the market in the short term.
"There's bound to be a short-term blow on the property market," Cheung said.

James Tin, managing director of Fortune Realty, said extra stamp duty on property sales within a year of purchase would be more effective because the duty would be charged irrespective of whether a profit had been made.
Some analysts said another effective measure to compress property prices could be a reduction of the maximum loan-value ratio to 60 percent from the present 70 percent.
But others, including Tin, argued that would be less feasible because it would also affect end-users directly.
Market players said property prices and transactions had already fallen since Leung's announcement.

Transaction prices of at least seven key housing estates across the territory fell one to four percent, while the number of transactions for 11 major housing estates slumped 10 to 40 percent after the news of imminent clampdown measures, Tin said.
John Yeung, a branch manager at Midland Realty, said transactions in some districts had fallen as much as 50 percent.
Some analysts also said they were concerned the new measures, if too drastic, would hit Hong Kong's economy.
Governor Chris Patten, who steps down at the handover, has also warned solutions to the booming property market will require a delicate touch.

"While you want to damp down speculation and any excessive increase in prices, you don't want to do anything which would damage the property market or investors' confidence in the medium and long term," Patten said on Monday.
The present administration launched major anti-speculation measures in 1994, dragging prices down by some 10 to 30 percent from their peaks.
